_comment: Course-level content for the Canvas front page. Edit the title here and re-run build_canvas_html.ps1.
title: Make Your Own Game
subtitle: Programming with Processing and the SpriteGame library
factStrip: 9 lessons + 3 bonus lessons  ·  No prior coding experience needed  ·  No points, no grades
overview: In this course you build a video game. Not a worksheet about video games — an actual game, with a character you draw yourself, that you can hand to somebody else and watch them play.

You start on the first day by putting something on the screen. In Lesson 2 you draw your character. After that, every single lesson gives that character something new: it moves, then you control it, then it gets a world to live in, then rules, then enemies. By Lesson 9 the game is **yours** — your character, your world, your rules.
You do not need any programming experience. Nothing here assumes you have ever seen code before.
goals: Write and run a Processing sketch from nothing
Create your own objects and tell them how to look and behave
Use variables, lists, loops, and `if` statements — because your game needed them, not because a test asked
Detect when things collide, and make the game react
Design a world with layers, terrain, and a look that is yours
Build a complete, playable game with win and lose conditions that somebody else can pick up and play

p: A **Lesson Page** — read it, follow the steps, get the code running. It has the new words, an explanation of how the new idea works, the starter code, and things to try.
An **Assignment** — where you turn your work in, check yourself against the stages, and write a sentence or two about what you did.

howItWorks.h: Every lesson ends with Make It Yours
p: This is the part that matters most, and it is not extra credit. The starter code is a starting point, not an answer. Changing it is the assignment.

Every lesson page and every assignment has a button that opens an AI helper for that lesson. It asks you questions and nudges you in the right direction — it will not just hand you the answer, because then you would not have learned anything.
Also: ask the person next to you, and ask your teacher. Both of those are allowed and both of them work.

stagesIntro: There are no points in this course, and no grades on your work. Instead, every assignment has the same four stages. They are a **map** of where you are and what to try next — not a score, and not a ranking.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: It is not running yet. Every lesson tells you the single most likely reason and exactly what to try next.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: The thing the lesson was about actually happens on your screen.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and you changed it on purpose, so it is yours. **This is the goal for everyone, every lesson.**

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and you took it somewhere the lesson never asked for. There is no fixed list for this one — that is the whole point of it.

stagesOutro: You can always go back, revise, and run it again. Nothing here is a one-shot test.
needList: **The SpriteGame library** — your teacher will help you install it if it is not already there
That is genuinely it. No account, no purchase, nothing to sign up for.
bonusNote: These three are extras. You can do them any time after the lesson listed, and skipping them will never block you — but each one makes your game noticeably more yours.
